name: Andrew Hamilton
occupation_background: Instructor of Computing and Data Science at Capilano University with a PhD in physics (University of Alberta); worked at CERN on the Higgs boson discovery and has lived in the US, Switzerland and South Africa. Husband and father of two; one-term councillor (2022-2026). Built bcmunicipaldata.org to let residents explore BC property tax data.
tagline: “Squamish is amazing.” Open consultation, respectful debate, transparent decisions.
top_priorities: Fiscally and environmentally sustainable core infrastructure
Fair and responsible development zoning
Reasonable and reliable recreation amenities
Realistic capital-project planning, cost forecasting and delivery
Focusing council on what is within municipal jurisdiction
Spending tax money efficiently

supports.text: Infill density over greenfield sprawl as the more economically and environmentally sustainable way to add housing supply

Parking reform: priced on-street parking (e.g. Cleveland Ave) to manage demand, with revenue returned to the affected area such as the Downtown BIA (his campaign site also calls for removing off-street parking minimums)
Better capital-project lifecycle budgeting - realistic cost forecasts, escalation mitigation, efficient execution
Delegating more development-permit decisions to staff for clarity and speed (moved the motion, Feb 2026)
Six-unit zoning with no parking minimum near future frequent transit
Bike paths, safe streets and more frequent transit so people can choose lower-carbon travel
Sunset clauses so upzoned projects get built in a reasonable time
Self-funded campaign under $500 with no donations

opposes.text: Free on-street parking and mandatory parking minimums, which he says create shortages and hide costs in food, housing and taxes

Most of the Garibaldi Estates pre-zoning - voted against three of the five bylaw votes on May 19 2026, objecting to pre-zoning for densities staff said were not financially viable and to treating one neighbourhood differently from the rest of town (he supported the two he judged viable: the ground-oriented residential zone and the District-led rezoning of 2163 Mamquam Road)
Permissive property tax exemptions for the Squamish Valley Golf Club and Sea to Sky Montessori (voted against, 2023-2024)
The 2024 Woodfibre LNG floatel permit as drafted - said the $2M security deposit was too low (he also voted against denying it)
Joining the Sue Big Oil class action (voted against at Oct 2023 committee of the whole; reasons not stated)
Council making advocacy its main focus - he calls advocacy 'a necessary role' but says council shouldn't spend all its time on it at the expense of what is within its jurisdiction

The proposed 10-year Woodfibre LNG tax agreement: voted to reject it (on Sept. 22, 2026 council voted 5–2 not to give the proposed 10-year Woodfibre LNG tax agreement its first three readings), saying fixing the company’s contribution would not make the community’s own future costs certain

growth.position: Not growing too fast: approve what meets community needs; clear rules set in advance; taller buildings by area-wide rezoning
growth.summary: States a general preference for infill density over greenfield sprawl and wants zoning that lets supply keep pace with demand. In practice he is a stickler for the zoned rules rather than a height opponent: he voted for the six-to-seven-storey Three Summits downtown development (Jan 2024) and seconded the six-unit transit-oriented zoning bylaw (Sept 2025), but voted against the seven-storey 38026 Second Avenue permit (June 2025) because it needed a height variance, saying council should stop granting height variances and change the zoning instead; he made the same point about the size, not the principle, of the Valleycliffe height variance. On the Garibaldi Estates pre-zoning (May 2026) he opposed three of the five bylaw votes and supported two, objecting to pre-zoning for densities staff said were not financially viable while stating he agreed with the neighbourhood plan itself.
growth.quote: Generally, I believe infill development (density) will lead to a more economically and environmentally sustainable community compared to greenfield development (sprawl).

housing_affordability.position: Strongly for a required share of below-market homes in big projects; more public money and land; match Airbnb rules to the Province
housing_affordability.summary: Sees zoning as council's most direct long-term lever and frames affordability as high demand meeting limited land. Argues removing parking minimums would relieve pressure on housing costs.
housing_affordability.quote: Let's reduce the pressure on the housing stock in our community, increase the housing stock in our community, and make it more affordable for folks to live here.

homelessness.position: More shelter and supportive housing, plus more to prevent street disorder; keep Under One Roof downtown; safety first
homelessness.summary: Part of the unanimous July 2026 vote for the Government Road supportive-housing lease, where he questioned BC Housing on building trust with the community. On the temporary housing site for the downtown encampment he urged residents to suggest alternatives once a site is announced.
homelessness.quote: If you don't think this site should be selected, please take the next step and suggest which sites should.

policing.position: Strongly for more bylaw officers downtown and mental-health crisis teams; in the middle on more RCMP
policing.summary: Andrew had said little in public about this before answering our questionnaire. Andrew’s own answers are below.

taxes_spending.position: Against capping taxes at inflation — it would mean cutting services; for borrowing for big projects; strongly for referendums above a set cost
taxes_spending.summary: Voted for the 2026-2035 plan despite misgivings about absorbing capital cost overruns. Names reforming how property tax rates are calculated as his top accomplishment, has the most property-tax dissents on council (mostly against permissive exemptions), moved a failed 2025 amendment to cut the Brennan Park line item, and warns projects such as the Pemberton-Laurelwood bridge are under-costed.
taxes_spending.quote: It's very easy to say somebody else should pay, but if somebody else is paying, they're part of our community, and we are paying.

environment_lng.position: Leans against the Woodfibre tax deal; won’t answer on Woodfibre permits, citing legal actions; core services before climate action
environment_lng.summary: The only member to vote against both denying and approving the floatel in April 2024 (he wanted a security deposit nearer $10M), then voted to reconsider and voted for the two-floatel permit in 2025; voted against the FortisBC lodge permit and against joining Sue Big Oil. Says climate change is human-caused and council's role is infrastructure that lets people choose lower-carbon options. On WLNG money, says the town has many capital needs to prioritise.
environment_lng.quote: There is no question in my mind that the Earth's climate is changing due to the carbon that humans are emitting into our atmosphere.

transportation.position: Strongly for regional transit, bike lanes and sidewalks
transportation.summary: His most detailed issue: pay parking where demand is highest ('not a revenue thing'), revenue kept local, and no parking minimums. Usually rides an e-bike when working in town and supports bike infrastructure and more frequent transit. Voted against the Dec 2024 motion that set the 30 km/h downtown limit and asked staff to scope a 40 km/h limit elsewhere; his reasons were not found in the sources reviewed.
transportation.quote: It's not a revenue thing. It's a management of the system.

economy.position: Leans toward cutting red tape and protecting industrial land
economy.summary: Andrew had said little in public about this before answering our questionnaire. Andrew’s own answers are below.

parking.position: Strongly for paid parking downtown, with no free pass for locals; against requiring parking in new buildings
parking.summary: Parking is his most developed issue. His campaign site endorses Donald Shoup's three reforms: charge the right price for on-street parking, spend the revenue on the metered streets, and 'Remove off-street parking requirements.' He told the Chief pay parking on Cleveland Avenue is 'not a revenue thing. It's a management of the system', with revenue possibly going to the Downtown BIA. On council he said his preference was paid parking 'everywhere, all at once', moved the defeated motions to make paid parking a 2025 priority and to study it community-wide, moved the amendment deleting the resident pass from the Darrell Bay pilot, seconded the six-unit/no-parking-minimum bylaw and removed the parking minimum for Garibaldi Highlands cafes. His site's 'ice cream' analogy argues a municipal parking lot ends up subsidised by property tax. A Squamish Reporter opinion piece says he supported a downtown parkade in 2022; I could not find the original 2022 statement.
parking.quote: It's not a revenue thing. It's a management of the system.

compass.rationale: Reasons explicitly from market economics (cites Sowell and Shoup; price parking, drop parking mandates, oppose tax exemptions, spending efficiency, realistic project costing) yet accepted double-digit tax increases as necessary. Accepts climate science and favours cycling/transit and supportive housing, but voted against Sue Big Oil and the 30 km/h zone and says advocacy, while necessary, should not crowd out work within council's own jurisdiction.

answer_notes.q1: The pace of new development approvals should be determined by whether development applications meet the community's needs, not by how quickly Council believes Squamish's population should grow.  Note that schools are outside the Council's jurisdiction.
answer_notes.q2: Taller buildings would require increased capacity in our fire department. Since a single building will not be capable of shouldering the cost burden of the increased fire service, a height increase should not be considered in a single-parcel rezoning but rather in a broad rezoning of an area.
answer_notes.q3: Adding density and opening new land are not mutually exclusive - this is not necessarily an either/or question. We will likely need both density and sprawl to address the housing needs in the coming decades. I believe increasing allowable density is an important first step, which is why I have supported it during the previous Council term.  Exploring greenfield expansion beyond the Growth Management Boundary should be done in the context of the upcoming OCP renewal.
answer_notes.q4: Below-market housing will not 'solve' our housing affordability challenge by itself. However, it is one tool in the municipal government's toolbox for keeping housing affordable. The benefits of below-market housing tend to increase over time as market rates rise while non-market rates remain flat (or don't rise as quickly). The mechanisms the municipality can use to achieve non-market housing are changing as we transition from Community Amenity Contributions (CAC) to Amenity Cost Charges (ACC).  We are in a transition period in not-for-profit housing, and I believe the long-term benefits will outweigh these short-term costs.
answer_notes.q5: It is clear that the current number of shelter beds and supportive housing units in Squamish isn't enough to serve the folks who need support. So yes, I believe Squamish needs more shelter and supportive-housing spaces. I also agree with the concerns raised by folks living near shelter spaces.  This issue is often framed as support for folks in need OR enforcement of laws and bylaws.  Like so many challenging conversations, I believe the best path forward will require both. We need to invest more in preventing street disorder to reduce the impact shelters and supportive housing have on surrounding neighbourhoods.
answer_notes.q6: As our population grows, we naturally need more police officers.  But I suspect the question is whether the current RCMP staffing level is sufficient for the current population. The RCMP has a method for determining the appropriate number of officers for a community, and the budgeted number falls within the normal-to-low range of their projections.  The current budget includes more officers because of significant recent and projected population increases.
answer_notes.q7: As a property taxpayer, I'd appreciate it if increases stayed at or below inflation. However, the cost of providing municipal services has risen faster than inflation in most BC communities.  Over the last 10 years, the average amount of property tax per capita has increased by about 4% (data from www.bcmunicipaldata.org), while inflation has averaged about 2.5% (data from Bank of Canada).   If we capped municipal taxes at inflation, we would see a deterioration in services. That doesn't mean delaying projects; it means not doing them. This isn't just a Squamish challenge; it's more systemic.
answer_notes.q8: Given the current legal actions against the District and the current members of Council, I will not respond to this question.
answer_notes.q9: I don't believe it should be a top priority.  Delivering core municipal services efficiently should always be our top priority.  The question doesn't specify who bears the cost or how much it is.  Energy efficiency in buildings costs more up front, but can save money in the long run. Beyond partnering with folks like BC Hydro, electric vehicle charging should be left in the private sector. Flood and wildfire protection are no longer "climate action", they are simply the reality of keeping our community safe(r) from the impacts of climate change.
answer_notes.q10: Rules should be clearly defined. If a developer wishes to vary a permit or rezone, then the process must be robust. The larger the variance, the more time it will take to carefully consider the impacts.
answer_notes.q37: Developers will build whatever people are willing to pay for. Developers build less parking because people generally don't want to pay the true cost of the space their vehicles occupy. This is partly because many people believe they should be allowed to park on the street for free. We do not expect to swim at the pool for free; why do we expect to park on the street for free?
answer_notes.q12: There is no question that the District will need to borrow to expand Brennan Park.  The District will need to borrow for any major capital investment.  The District is currently close to its debt-servicing limit.  Debt-servicing is the percentage of annual municipal revenue required to pay principal and interest on debt.  We are currently at 17% (as of the 2026 budget), and we have a self-imposed policy limit of 20%. The provincial limit is 25%.  We could increase our self-imposed limit, but that may limit our ability to manage any emergency borrowing in an unforeseen event.
answer_notes.q18: Moving the challenges elsewhere would simply cost a lot of money.  We must find a way to manage street disorder.
answer_notes.q31: We need both shelter and enforcement.
answer_notes.q34: It is a very small amount of money to help make people feel welcome.
answer_notes.q15: This is an ill-formed question; land can serve many purposes, not just housing or cash.
answer_notes.q16: I believe we should align our STR policies with the provincial regulations.
answer_notes.q17:
People needing social assistance should receive it. But that is a provincial jurisdiction. 
People who don't need social assistance should contribute to municipal infrastructure costs, after all, "Everybody Poops" [Taro Gomi].
answer_notes.q22: This question assumes Brennan Park is the next facility on the capital projects list.  That decision has not been made.  If the question is asking whether I think borrowing is generally appropriate for capital project funding, then the answer is absolutely yes.
answer_notes.q24: Higher than what?  We already require Level 4 Zero-Carbon step code.
answer_notes.q25:
Please read "The High Cost of Free Parking" by Donald Shoup and/or Paved Paradise by Henry Grabar.  
Parking, like many things in life, comes down to a pick-two-of-three: free, available, or close.  Pick two.
answer_notes.q36: I agree that downtown might need more parking. I disagree that the District should build a parking garage.
answer_notes.q38: I believe exempting locals defeats the purpose of managing demand.
answer_notes.q26: They are way cheaper than roads. For each person who rides or walks to where they need to go, one more space opens up on the road for those who drive - either by choice or by necessity.
answer_notes.q27: Make a plan.  Stick to it.  If you see the plan isn't working, change it.  The whole plan, not just one parcel.
answer_notes.q28: I think we need to spend more of the funding that we have already allocated.
answer_notes.q29: It depends on what type of land you are talking about.  For fee simple private land, zoning should remain the District of Squamish's responsibility.  For publicly owned land, yes, decision-making should be shared.
answer_notes.q30: This question mixes two related, but mutually exclusive, ideas.  We should actively work to expand the amount of space that is zoned for childcare.  This is not the same as subsidized childcare.  Childcare should remain a provincial responsibility or move under the School Board's responsibility.
answer_notes.q32: Safety for everyone.  Encampments are not safe for the folks living in them.
answer_notes.q33: Low income, yes.  Supportive, no.   Supportive (as the name suggests) requires a support system.  Spreading that support to many locations would cost more than hosting it in one place; thus, we would provide less support in a distributed model.  Low-income housing does not require continued support; thus, it can be mixed throughout the town.
answer_notes.q35: It is not clear that this is still the case.  The decriminalization exemption expired on January 31, 2026, and will not be renewed (according to BCCDC).

own_words.homelessness: Support Heart and Hearth.  Support Bylaw enforcement.  The cost to have a meaningful impact is unknowable.

name: Janice DesJardins
incumbent_role: Not an incumbent (no record of prior council runs found)
occupation_background: Long-time Squamish resident and volunteer whose family roots in town date to 1912; her grandfather Alex Munro founded the volunteer fire department and was its first chief. Seniors and long-term-care advocate: Vice Chair of the Vancouver Coastal Association of Family Councils, Co-Chair of the VCH Regional Resident & Family Councils, member of the Independent Long Term Care Councils Association of BC and the Seniors Aging at Home Community Network. Previously sat on the District's first tourism plan committee and with the Squamish Estuary Conservation Society on the Estuary Management Plan.
tagline: Time for Change! Livability, Affordability, Fiscal Responsibility, Accountability — using Common Sense!
top_priorities: Livability: housing and density, parking, recreation facilities, transit, safety, property taxes
Affordability: help for workers earning below the living wage; attract an 'economic engine'
Fiscal Responsibility: zero-based budgeting, strive for zero property tax increases, limit debt
Accountability & Transparency: referendums on major capital projects, council taking authority back from staff
A land bank for employee housing and housing society projects

supports.text: Striving for zero annual property tax increases, using zero-based budgeting and focusing on needs not wants
Referendums on major capital projects (e.g. the public safety building)
Putting high density in new developments, and developing outside the existing OCP boundary to get out of the flood plain onto higher ground
Starting a land bank now (possibly via Crown land) for future employee housing and housing society projects, following Whistler's model
Attracting industry as an 'economic engine' that brings well-paid jobs and tax revenue
A downtown parking committee of stakeholders plus one councillor; using empty stalls in downtown residential buildings
Renegotiating the Woodfibre LNG 10-year tax agreement under a new council to get more money for Squamish
More openness: a regular 'Council Corner' newspaper column, all letters to council on the agenda, public meetings on land use, an independent committee for code-of-conduct complaints
An annual 'How are we doing?' questionnaire to residents
'Missing middle' housing — townhouses, duplexes, triplexes and low-rise apartments — throughout the community, with updated zoning and streamlined approvals
Protecting existing rental stock, incentives for purpose-built rental, and stopping the loss of affordable units to short-term rentals and renovictions
Higher affordable-housing requirements and stronger community-benefit agreements in new developments, plus a Housing Action Plan with targets, timelines and public progress reports
More frequent buses on core routes, evening and weekend service, better coverage of newer neighbourhoods, and exploring express regional service with BC Transit and TransLink
A Seniors Advisory Council (as council did for youth) and implementing the Age Friendly Community Plan council endorsed
Mayor and council lobbying Victoria 'long and hard' for the cancelled 152-bed long-term care facility, and directing staff to seek private and BC Housing partners for more assisted living
Ground-level, wheelchair-accessible seniors' housing near shops and services, with Eagle Grove as the model and new developments contributing land or money
Funding core services and the infrastructure maintenance backlog before adding new programs; a business case, competitive procurement and honest over-budget reporting for every major spend
A needs assessment and public consultation before deciding whether to repair, renew or replace Brennan Park, paid for through grants, partnerships, naming rights and phased financing
Moving restaurant patios off street parking stalls and banning food trucks from parking on Cleveland and 2nd Avenues between Victoria and Pemberton
Implementing the District's existing Heritage Management Strategy before development pressure makes it too late

opposes.text: High density in existing, long-established neighbourhoods that do not want it
The Woodfibre LNG 10-Year Agreement in Principle as negotiated ("That is not a good deal for Squamish")
The alternative approval process for borrowing, which she called "a joke", citing the public works building she says came in $19 million over budget
Staff having too much authority ("Council have given Staff too much authority and council must take it back")
Further increases to District debt and continued property tax increases
Housing vulnerable seniors together with people with serious mental-health and substance-use disorders in the proposed Government Road supportive housing project (2025 letter)
Removing any more parking stalls near seniors' facilities and seniors' housing — 'particularly not to put in bike lanes'
Deferred maintenance, which she calls 'a debt that future taxpayers will pay with interest'

growth.summary: Wants high density placed in new developments rather than in established neighbourhoods that do not want it, and supports development outside the current OCP boundary to get off the flood plain onto higher ground.
growth.quote: High density should be in new developments and not in existing, long established neighbourhoods who do not want it. I believe in development outside of our existing OCP in order to get outside of the flood plain and to higher ground.

housing_affordability.position: Land bank for employee and housing-society housing (Whistler model)
housing_affordability.summary: Says Squamish has done the paperwork on affordable housing but barely delivered, and that zoning reform alone does not make anything affordable. Wants a land bank, possibly from Crown land, for employee housing, co-op style ownership and housing society projects, citing Whistler. Her site's housing page adds: 'missing middle' townhouses and low-rise 'throughout the community' with streamlined approvals, protecting rental stock from short-term rentals and renovictions, higher affordable-housing requirements in new developments, and a Housing Action Plan with targets and public reporting.
housing_affordability.quote: Zoning reform makes building possible, it doesn't make anything affordable. That takes land, covenants, and capital. And those are the three boxes still unticked in Squamish.

homelessness.position: Opposed mixing seniors with mental-health/addictions clients in the Government Road supportive housing proposal
homelessness.summary: In a July 2025 letter she said she supports safe, affordable housing for people in need, including people experiencing homelessness, but called it a 'grave mistake' to house vulnerable seniors with people who may be actively struggling with serious mental-health and substance-use disorders, and argued addictions care needs specialized, secure facilities. No 2026 campaign statement on shelters or encampments found.
homelessness.quote: This is not about NIMBYism. It's about responsible, evidence-based, and compassionate planning.

policing.summary: Lists 'Safety' as a key issue she will address later in the campaign; no details yet on RCMP, bylaw or alternatives.

taxes_spending.position: Strive for zero property tax increases; limit debt; referendums on big projects
taxes_spending.summary: Calls for spending discipline, zero-based budgeting, needs over wants, market value for District land sales, limits on new debt and referendums on major capital projects. Asked by the Chief what she would cut to reach zero, she said she was not sure yet and that an inventory of all spending was needed.
taxes_spending.quote: Annually, we should strive for zero increases in property taxes. Zero based budgeting can get us there.

environment_lng.position: Renegotiate the WLNG tax deal for more money; sees WLNG as the town's only economic engine
environment_lng.summary: Does not support the Woodfibre LNG 10-Year Agreement in Principle, saying more money could be negotiated and a new council should reset the relationship, while describing WLNG as currently Squamish's one and only economic engine that the town has to work with. Past volunteer on the Squamish Estuary Management Plan. No climate-policy statement found.
environment_lng.quote: This should be done with a new council who does a reset on the relationship with WLNG.

transportation.position: More downtown parking now; more frequent buses, evening/weekend service and express regional links
transportation.summary: Says retail, medical-office and downtown employees need parking options immediately; would explore managing empty stalls in downtown residential buildings and on-street cafe stalls, via a stakeholder parking committee with one councillor. Lists transit as a key issue but has not yet published details. Her transit page calls for more frequent service on core routes, evening and weekend hours, coverage of newer neighbourhoods, better shelters and real-time arrival information, and exploring express regional connections with BC Transit and TransLink. She also wants new developments located and designed to support transit.
transportation.quote: Retail employees, medical offices, and downtown employees all need parking options immediately.

economy.summary: Wants to attract industry that provides well-paid jobs and tax revenue, noting the loss of forestry and a living wage ($28/hr) far above minimum wage. Says retail and industrial tax rates are considerably higher than residential and push businesses to close.
economy.quote: I want to attract industry that will function as an 'economic engine', providing new jobs and attracting new business.

parking.position: 'Nowhere near enough parking spaces downtown'; wants bylaws to require adequate stalls for all housing, and a parking committee to look at angle parking, an employee lot and Loggers Lane
parking.summary: Parking is the first issue on her platform. She says high-density development has pushed residents' second cars onto the street and displaced downtown employees into the two-hour zones. Immediate steps: move restaurant patios off street stalls and ban food trucks from parking on Cleveland and Second between Victoria and Pemberton. She would strike a community Parking Committee to explore angle parking, a dedicated employee lot, angle parking on the old Loggers Lane rail bed and reopening side streets to parking, and task it with 'updating parking bylaws to require adequate stalls for all forms of housing — including suites' and investigating permit parking, pay parking and one-way streets. She also wants the one-stall-per-suite rule enforced. On a parkade: 'Maybe we don't need a parkade — but we do have to investigate all options first.'
parking.quote: There are nowhere near enough parking spaces downtown. High-density development has pushed residents with two vehicles onto the street, displacing the spots once used by downtown employees.

compass.rationale: Zero tax increases, zero-based budgeting, debt limits, referendums on capital spending and attracting industry place her clearly on the fiscal-restraint side, tempered by support for a public land bank for non-market housing and a harder bargain with WLNG. Socially, she defends established neighbourhoods against density and opposed a mixed supportive-housing model on safety grounds, while stating support for housing people in need; no policing position found.

answer_notes.q1: I think Squamish should keep being open to growth while making sure our policies and practices keep pace, from building design and parking to active transportation, recreation and infrastructure
answer_notes.q2: I support higher density downtown, but would like to see good design, more useable commercial spaces, and realistic parking requirements.
answer_notes.q3: There is already quite a bit of undeveloped land within Squamish’s growth boundary, so I am cautious about one-off decisions to expand it. These are conversations that are best had as part of an Official Community Plan process, which will be coming up during this Council’s term.
answer_notes.q8: My expectation is that WLNG is accountable to all levels of government with regular reporting and responsiveness to concerns. I expect WLNG to help pay for the District’s 10-year capital plan either through taxation or a fair tax deal, and have not seen enough analysis to be convinced that the current tax deal in front of Council achieves this.

compass.rationale: Public statements are pragmatic and non-ideological: balance the finances, plan civic facility renewal, plan outdoor recreation, hold developers to parking rules unless benefits are delivered. answer_notes.q1:
Development is an important source of revenue for the District, and it helps fund the services and amenities our community relies on. However, residents must always come first. This means making sure our infrastructure keeps pace with growth.
As we welcome new development, we need to ensure that roads, water distribution systems, sewer infrastructure, parks, recreation facilities, and community services are planned and funded appropriately.
My goal is simple: support responsible growth that benefits the entire community, ensure development contributes its fair share, and maintain the quality of life that makes Squamish such a great place to live.
answer_notes.q2: Our views are one of Squamish's greatest assets. They define our community, contribute to our quality of life, and are a big part of why people choose to live here. I support responsible growth, but not at the expense of the character and natural beauty that make Squamish special.
answer_notes.q3:
To be honest, I'm not convinced the answer is simply more density everywhere, and I'm not convinced the answer is opening new land everywhere either.
I think it's a conversation worth having as a community.
If we're going to consider new neighbourhoods, it needs to be done responsibly, with meaningful community engagement and more opportunities for Council to be involved in those discussions. These decisions will shape Squamish for generations, and residents deserve to have a real voice in them.
I'm open to exploring new areas for housing if there's a clear benefit to the community. That could mean creating more housing options, improving affordability, or delivering new amenities and infrastructure that make life better for residents.
But growth for the sake of growth isn't enough. I want to know how it will benefit the people who already live here, how we'll pay for the infrastructure, and whether it helps us build a stronger community.
At the end of the day, my focus is making sure growth works for residents first. If opening new land helps us achieve that, then it's a discussion I'm willing to have.
answer_notes.q4:
I'll be honest, creating non-market housing is not an area where I have deep expertise.
I tend to look at this issue through the eyes of the average taxpayer. I want to help people, and I recognize that many residents are struggling with housing affordability. I also believe that local government has an obligation to support vulnerable residents and help where it can.
At the same time, I think municipalities have been asked to carry more responsibility for housing without always receiving the support and funding we need from senior levels of government. That's a challenge we must acknowledge.
For me, it's about finding balance. We need a community that is affordable and inclusive, but we also need to invest in the infrastructure, parks, recreation facilities, and services that make Squamish a great place to live.
I don't know exactly where that balance lies, and I think it's different for every project. What I do know is that the District needs a strong foundation if we're going to help others effectively. The stronger we are as a municipality, the more we can do to support residents who need a helping hand.
I'm open to supporting non-market housing initiatives when there is a clear community benefit, strong partnerships, and a responsible plan that makes sense for both current residents and future generations.
answer_notes.q5:
I think we need to find a balance.
Supporting the most vulnerable members of our community should always be part of the conversation. Everyone deserves dignity, safety, and access to the services they need to get back on their feet.
At the same time, we have a responsibility to residents, families, and businesses who want safe and welcoming neighbourhoods. That's why I believe supportive housing needs to be paired with the right services, support staff, and community safety resources.
I support expanding supportive housing, but I also believe location matters and each proposal should be evaluated carefully. I don't think there is a one-size-fits-all solution.
We need honest conversations with residents, service providers, and the people who will be living in these homes. My goal would be to find solutions that help our most vulnerable residents while maintaining the quality of life that people expect in their neighbourhoods.
I don't claim to have all the answers, but I do believe we need to keep working together to find solutions that are compassionate, practical, and work for the entire community.
answer_notes.q6:
The District already spends millions of taxpayer dollars each year on RCMP services, so the question isn't always whether we need more officers. Sometimes it's about how those officers are deployed and how connected they are to our community.
We need to make sure our RCMP members have the tools, training, and resources they need to succeed. Policing today is far more complex than it used to be. Officers are increasingly dealing with mental health challenges, addiction, homelessness, and social issues that weren't traditionally part of policing.
To me, community policing is about relationships. Residents should know their local officers. Businesses should feel heard when they raise concerns. People should feel comfortable reporting issues before they become bigger problems.
I also think we need to be realistic. The RCMP cannot solve every social issue on its own. Strong community safety comes from partnerships between police, outreach workers, health services, businesses, and residents all working together.
If elected, I would advocate for a stronger community policing presence in Squamish. I want to see officers out in the community, building relationships, understanding local concerns, and focusing on prevention whenever possible. At the same time, I want to make sure taxpayers are receiving good value for the significant investment they're already making in public safety.
At the end of the day, people want to feel safe in their neighbourhoods, safe in our parks and trails, and safe walking through our downtown. That's what I will focus on.
answer_notes.q7:
Core infrastructure is my passion, and I know firsthand how expensive it is when a community falls behind on maintaining it.
For me, the priority is clear. Without reliable drinking water, sewer and storm systems, roads, and flood protection, nothing else works. We can build homes, attract businesses, and plan for growth, but if the infrastructure underneath it can't support that growth, we're setting ourselves up for failure.
Our infrastructure is aging, and we need to be honest about that. I will push to maintain and replace these critical assets in the most cost-effective way possible. These systems don't generate revenue. They cost money to build, operate, and maintain, but they are essential to public safety and quality of life.
I believe Council has a responsibility to stretch every taxpayer dollar as far as possible. That means better asset management, long-term planning, prioritizing maintenance before emergency repairs, and constantly looking for grants, partnerships, and efficiencies before turning to taxpayers for more money.
Keeping tax increases affordable is important, but I don't believe an arbitrary commitment to keeping taxes below inflation should come at the expense of critical infrastructure or public safety. Delaying necessary investments often costs more in the long run.
My approach will be to look for savings first, improve efficiency wherever possible, and make sure every dollar is spent wisely. If additional funding is truly necessary to protect essential infrastructure or public safety, then I believe we need to have an honest conversation with residents about why it's needed and what benefits it will deliver.
At the end of the day, my goal is simple: protect the infrastructure that keeps our community safe, spend taxpayer money responsibly, and leave Squamish in better condition than we found it.
answer_notes.q23:
Based on the information available, I would have supported the agreement.

For me, this is less about whether someone supports or opposes the project and more about responsible financial management on behalf of taxpayers.

The District has the authority to set its industrial tax rate, but the fact remains that we are currently involved in litigation. At some point, the courts will provide direction on what is reasonable, and future tax rates will likely need to reflect that outcome. If the District is successful, that's great. If not, we could face significant costs, uncertainty, and the challenge of establishing a new tax rate framework moving forward.

I also recognize that litigation is expensive. The longer disputes continue, the more uncertainty exists for both the District and Woodfibre LNG. As someone who believes in long-term planning, I see value in reducing uncertainty whenever possible.

One of the things that appealed to me about the agreement was the predictability. A guaranteed revenue stream over ten years would have provided certainty for financial planning, infrastructure investment, and asset management. When you're managing major infrastructure projects, predictable funding allows you to plan better, prioritize work, and often save money over the long term.

I also understand that tax agreements between governments and large industrial projects are not uncommon. They can provide stability for both parties and help establish a workable long-term relationship.

That doesn't mean we leave money on the table without asking questions. The District has a responsibility to negotiate in the best interests of residents. But given the certainty of the proposed revenue, the cost and uncertainty of ongoing litigation, and the importance of maintaining a productive relationship with one of the largest taxpayers in the community, I would have supported the agreement.

At the end of the day, my responsibility is to look at long-term financial sustainability. Pre
answer_notes.q8:
I would have supported the agreement because I want the District to have a strong, workable relationship with Woodfibre LNG. That relationship should be respectful, accountable, and built on clear expectations from both sides.
Whether people support the project or not, the reality is that if the facility operates successfully, it will be part of our community for decades. I believe we can often achieve more through constructive engagement and partnership than through constant conflict and litigation.
A stable relationship creates opportunities for ongoing dialogue about community benefits, infrastructure investments, local employment, environmental accountability, and other issues that matter to residents. That doesn't mean giving anyone a free pass. It means holding partners accountable while working together toward outcomes that benefit Squamish.
My preference is to build relationships that are firm but respectful, because I believe that approach is more likely to deliver long-term benefits for our community than continued uncertainty and legal disputes.
answer_notes.q9:
For me, taking care of basic needs comes first. People need safe drinking water, reliable roads, effective sewer and storm systems, flood protection, and affordable services. That's the foundation of a healthy community.
I believe climate change is real, and we are already seeing its impacts through extreme weather, wildfire risk, and flooding. We need to do our part, but we also need to be realistic about costs and priorities.
My approach is to focus on climate actions that deliver practical benefits to residents and strengthen our community. Investments in flood protection, wildfire preparedness, resilient infrastructure, and energy efficiency help protect people and property while preparing us for the future.
At the same time, I don't believe every climate initiative should take priority over core infrastructure or essential services. Council has a responsibility to manage taxpayer dollars carefully and make sure we're getting value for our investments.
I would support setting clear priorities, establishing realistic budgets, and focusing on projects that provide measurable benefits to residents. If we can't provide reliable water, sewer, roads, and public safety, then we've missed the mark.
My priority will always be protecting the infrastructure and services that keep our community safe. Climate action is important, but it needs to be balanced with affordability and the basic needs of the residents who call Squamish home.
answer_notes.q10:
Absolutely, 
This is one of the areas where I would like to focus my energy as a councillor because the benefits are felt across the entire community. Faster and more predictable approvals help businesses invest, create jobs, build housing, and reduce costs.
I also think we need to recognize that many delays are not caused by bad intentions. Sometimes applications are complex. Sometimes applicants don't fully understand what information is required. Sometimes staff are working with limited resources and competing priorities.
That's why I believe the solution is not simply removing rules. The solution is creating a process that is clear, efficient, and easy to follow.
We need to give Municipal Hall the tools, staffing, and resources necessary to succeed. We need a process that is easy for staff to administer, easy for applicants to understand, and designed to lead to successful outcomes.
A good process should clearly explain requirements upfront, identify issues early, reduce unnecessary back-and-forth, and provide applicants with realistic timelines and expectations. When everyone understands the process, projects move forward faster and with fewer surprises.
We still need rules that protect residents, neighbourhoods, and the environment. But there is no reason those protections can't exist alongside a streamlined and efficient approval system.
At the end of the day, I want a District that is known for being professional, responsive, and easy to work with. When you have a well-designed process, residents are happier, businesses are happier, applicants are happier, and staff are happier. That's a win for everyone.
answer_notes.q11:
I support investing local tax dollars in regional transit because it has a direct benefit for Squamish residents. Better transit connections to Vancouver and Whistler could help workers, students, businesses, and visitors while reducing traffic on the Sea-to-Sky Highway.
That said, regional transit is expensive and comes with challenges. Ridership is often heavier in one direction than the other, which can impact efficiency and operating costs. There are also practical considerations around comfort, luggage storage, bike capacity, and the type of service being offered.
My approach would be to look for the most cost-effective solution possible. Before asking local taxpayers to shoulder the full burden, I would want to explore partnerships with the Province, BC Transit, neighbouring communities, major employers, and tourism organizations.
If we can share costs and responsibilities, we have a much better chance of delivering a service that is affordable, sustainable, and available sooner rather than later.
I believe regional transit is worth pursuing, but it needs to be done responsibly. We need a service that works for residents, makes financial sense, and provides long-term value to the community. As with any major investment, I would want to see a solid business case, realistic ridership projections, and a clear funding strategy before moving forward.
answer_notes.q37:
I do not support parking variances that reduce the minimum parking requirements for new developments.
In my view, the current parking requirements are already close to the minimum. They were designed with the expectation that more people will use active transportation and transit in the future. While I support those goals, the reality is that many residents still rely on their vehicles every day.
We are already seeing the impacts of parking shortages in parts of downtown Squamish. When developments don't provide enough parking, the problem doesn't disappear. It gets pushed onto neighbouring streets and existing residents.
I believe developers should provide adequate parking for the people who will live in their buildings. If a development brings new residents, it should also help accommodate their parking needs.
That doesn't mean we stop investing in transit, cycling, or walkability. We should continue supporting those options, but we also need to be realistic about how people live and travel today.
My position is simple: future development should help solve our parking challenges, not add to them. As a councillor, I would support clear and consistent parking requirements that protect existing neighbourhoods while ensuring growth remains responsible and sustainable.
answer_notes.q12:
We absolutely need a new recreation centre. We need another pool, more ice time, and additional recreation space to support a growing community. Recreation is important on many levels. It keeps people active, teaches our kids essential skills like swimming, supports physical and mental health, and provides the quality of life that residents expect.
The challenge is how we pay for it.
I know the community has been waiting a long time for improvements to Brennan Park, but I am cautious about taking on significant new debt given the financial pressures the District is already facing. Before borrowing tens of millions of dollars, I want to make sure we have explored every available option.
I would like to see the District get creative and investigate partnerships with private industry, senior levels of government, community organizations, and potentially neighbouring communities. Other municipalities have successfully used partnership models to help deliver recreation facilities, and I think those examples are worth exploring.
My goal would be to deliver these amenities sooner rather than later while minimizing the financial burden on taxpayers. If we can find a way to share costs, reduce risk, and accelerate delivery, that's a conversation worth having.
I support investing in recreation, but I also believe we need to be responsible with public finances. We all want these facilities, but we need a plan that the community can afford.
At the end of the day, doing nothing isn't an option. Squamish has outgrown its existing recreation facilities. The question isn't whether we need more recreation infrastructure. The question is how we deliver it in a way that is financially responsible and sustainable for future generations.
answer_notes.q18:
I believe we need to take a serious look at how supportive housing and related services are distributed throughout the community.
I fully support helping vulnerable people and ensuring they have access to shelter, housing, and the services they need. At the same time, I think we need to be honest about the challenges that residents, businesses, and visitors have raised regarding the concentration of services in the downtown core.
Downtown is where a lot of the community comes together. It's home to Municipal Hall, the library, local businesses, restaurants, community events, and many of the places we encourage visitors to explore. It's also an area where residents should feel comfortable living, working, and spending time.
My concern is not with the people who need help. My concern is whether we have the right balance and the right support systems in place. I think it's reasonable to review whether our current approach is working for everyone and whether services could be delivered more effectively.
I would support a community discussion that includes residents, businesses, service providers, and the people using these services. The goal should be finding solutions that support vulnerable individuals while also maintaining a safe, welcoming, and vibrant downtown.
I also believe supportive housing needs to be paired with appropriate supports, community safety measures, and enforcement when necessary. Housing alone is not enough.
At the end of the day, I want a compassionate community that helps those in need, but I also want a downtown that residents can be proud of, businesses can thrive in, and visitors want to return to. I believe we can achieve both if we're willing to have honest conversations and work together on practical solutions.
answer_notes.q31:
This is one of the toughest challenges facing our community.
I understand why people want encampments cleared. They can create safety concerns for the people living there, nearby residents, businesses, and the environment. But simply clearing an encampment without another option usually just moves the problem somewhere else.
I believe we need an immediate solution that balances compassion with accountability, while working toward a long-term solution that improves safety and helps restore prosperity in our downtown. We need to support people who are struggling, but we also need to make sure residents, businesses, and visitors feel safe in our community.
I want to see stronger community policing and more support for the RCMP in dealing with repeat offenders who are creating safety concerns. We need to help people who want help, but there also need to be consequences for those who continue to harm the community.
If there were an easy solution, we would have found it already. My focus will be on improving public safety, increasing accountability, supporting local businesses, and working toward long-term housing and support solutions that treat people with dignity and respect.
answer_notes.q34:
I think it's important that everyone feels welcome and that they belong in Squamish.
Community symbols, proclamations, and other forms of recognition can help with that, but right now the District is facing significant financial pressures and major infrastructure needs.
I believe our spending should be proportional to the challenges we're facing. We should focus on practical and affordable ways to build inclusion today, and those ideas should come directly from the people and groups looking for that support. They know best what would make a meaningful difference in their lives.
As our financial position improves, we can invest more in initiatives that strengthen community connection and belonging.
My goal is to find the right balance: making sure everyone feels welcome while being responsible with taxpayer dollars.

own_words.one_thing:
If I could achieve one thing in four years, it would be to strengthen Municipal Hall.
That's where the foundation for everything we want to achieve as a community is built. It's where we plan projects, deliver services, support businesses, manage growth, and make decisions that affect every resident in Squamish.
I believe a strong community starts with a strong foundation, and that foundation is our staff. Whether it's the people repairing water mains, maintaining parks, collecting garbage, issuing permits, operating equipment, supporting residents at the front counter, or managing projects behind the scenes, they are the people who keep Squamish running every day.
I want our employees to know that Council has their back. That means providing the tools, technology, training, equipment, staffing levels, and leadership they need to be successful. Better GIS resources, better asset management, stronger public works support, and better internal processes all help staff do their jobs more efficiently and safely.
This isn't about hiring more people every time we have a new idea. It's about building a well-functioning organization and giving our employees the resources they need to succeed. I believe both management and frontline staff play critical roles, and the best results happen when everyone is working toward the same goals.
I also believe that when people feel supported, respected, and equipped to do their jobs well, it creates a stronger workplace culture. Good communication, strong leadership, and mutual respect help build trust throughout the organization. My hope is that by investing in our people and giving them the resources they need, we can make collaboration easier at every level, including future labour negotiations.
When staff have the tools they need and leadership they can count on, they provide better service, solve problems faster, and take pride in their work. When Municipal Hall succeeds, the entire community benefits.
My goal is simple: build a Municipal Hall that delivers excellent service, supports its employees, and gives Squamish the strong foundation it needs to thrive for years to come.
own_words.say_no:
I strongly believe Squamish needs to protect its commercial and industrial lands.
While I understand the pressure to create more housing, our community also needs places for businesses to operate, local jobs to grow, and industry to thrive. Commercial and industrial lands are important for our long-term economic health and help generate the tax revenue needed to support municipal services.
Because of that, and despite the difficult choices involved, I would not support rezoning commercial or industrial lands for residential use. Once those lands are gone, it's very difficult to get them back.
I believe we need to find housing solutions that preserve the employment lands and economic opportunities that future generations will depend on.
own_words.homelessness:
The first thing I would say is that the current situation isn't working. It's not working for residents, it's not working for businesses, and it's not working for many of the people who are struggling.
I don't believe simply clearing encampments is a solution. If people have nowhere else to go, we're often just moving the problem from one street or neighbourhood to another.
I believe we need an immediate approach that balances compassion with accountability. We need to support people who are struggling, but we also need to make sure residents, businesses, and visitors feel safe in our community.
In the short term, I would support stronger community policing, more support for the RCMP in dealing with repeat offenders, and better coordination between police, outreach workers, and social services. We need to help people who want help, but there also need to be consequences for those who continue to create safety concerns and harm the community.
Longer term, I think we need to look at a more practical solution than unmanaged encampments. That could include a purpose-built site in an appropriate location with less impact on residential neighbourhoods and businesses. I would be interested in exploring options such as micro-units, tiny homes, or a managed camping facility with security, basic services, washrooms, and access to mental health, addiction, and housing supports.
As for cost, I don't believe Squamish taxpayers should carry that burden alone. I would first pursue provincial and federal funding, along with partnerships with service providers, because these are regional and societal challenges, not just municipal ones. In many cases, the cost of doing nothing is already being paid through policing, emergency response, cleanups, environmental impacts, and reduced business activity.
If there were an easy solution, we would have found it already. My goal is to improve public safety, support local businesses, increase accountability, and create a pathway for people to move from encampments into a safer and more stable environment.
own_words.differently:
One recent decision where I likely would have voted differently was the proposed agreement with Woodfibre LNG. Council voted to reject the deal, but based on the information available, I would have supported it.
For me, the decision came down to financial certainty, risk management, and long-term planning. The agreement would have provided predictable revenue for ten years, ended costly litigation, and allowed the District to focus on priorities like infrastructure, recreation, transportation, and emergency preparedness instead of court proceedings.
I understand why others disagreed, and I respect that decision. However, I believe certainty has value. A guaranteed revenue stream would have helped us plan ahead and potentially save money through better long-term asset management.
I also believe in building strong, respectful, and accountable relationships with major employers and taxpayers. Whether people support the project or not, if Woodfibre LNG operates successfully, it will be part of our community for decades. I think we can often achieve more through constructive engagement than through ongoing conflict.
That doesn't mean giving anyone a free pass. It means negotiating firmly, protecting the interests of residents, and working toward solutions that provide long-term benefits for the community. In this case, I would likely have come to a different conclusion than the current Council.
own_words.disagree:
I would start by listening.
We may have different views on an issue, but that doesn't mean we can't have a respectful conversation. I want to understand why you feel the way you do, and I'd hope you'd want to understand my perspective as well.
Maybe one of us changes our mind. Maybe neither of us does. That's okay.
Personally, I believe strong beliefs are important, but they're not the most important thing. The most important thing is continuing the conversation and working together to find solutions. Local government isn't about winning arguments. It's about bringing people together, finding common ground where we can, and moving the community forward.
Even when I disagree with someone, I want them to know they'll be heard, treated with respect, and that I'll take their concerns seriously. That's how I try to approach every issue, and that's the kind of councillor I want to be.

name: Laura Prosko

She says she was recruited to move to Squamish in 2020 to work on Woodfibre LNG (until May 2025). Serves on the Westwinds Seniors Board and the International Cultural Heritage Society, previously served with the Squamish Chamber of Commerce, has been involved with Rotary, and is trained as an Emergency Support Services Officer and Information Officer.

name: Chris Ryan
occupation_background: First came to the Sea to Sky to work in the summers of 1986–88 and moved back full-time in 1993. Studied marketing, retail management and ski racing at Sheridan College, then worked five years in real estate. For about 30 years he sold advertising to Sea to Sky small businesses (Whistler Question, Whistler This Week, Western phone directories) and ran a seasonal property-maintenance company for 20 years. Raised his partner’s two sons in Pemberton; moved to Squamish in 2018 (Garibaldi, then downtown). Now works in renewable energy solutions and landscapes one day a week in summer. Says he will miss the Oct 5 all-candidates debate for a family wedding out of province.
tagline: “A voice for common sense & action in Squamish.”
top_priorities: Work with the Province and other governments instead of fighting them
Parking, and a second road in and out of downtown
Whistler-style housing for locals and seniors
Get Woodfibre LNG to help pay for community projects
Look after streets, curbs and drains to avoid big repair bills
Safety downtown

supports.text: Working with the Province on its projects, so senior governments will help fund Squamish’s own projects
Buying the Loggers Lane rail line to extend the Feather Park bike lane to Hunter Place Road, with angled parking that visitors pay for and residents and workers use with a permit
Paving Bailey Street and opening it to the business park as a second route in and out of downtown, with paved parking for Bailey Street residents
Adopting the Whistler Housing Authority model (rent covenants and caps on resale prices) and revisiting the Cheema land proposal for “high density, low sprawl” family housing
Turning vacant office space that builders must include in residential buildings into affordable and seniors’ housing
Working with Woodfibre LNG to help pay for Brennan Park, reopening the Bailey Street tennis courts, and a youth skate/bike/ball court in Garibaldi
Renewable energy on municipal buildings, schools and new construction
A winter bus to Darrell Bay (for example three times a day) and a transit link joining the Sea to Sky communities
Regular weeding and maintenance of downtown curbs, sidewalks and storm drains to prevent costly damage
Requiring builders to provide parking instead of paying cash-in-lieu, and to keep vacant lots tidy

opposes.text: The location of the safe injection site beside the public library, a Montessori daycare, a park and homes — says it “needs to be removed”
The trailer-and-tent encampment on the vacant lot at Loggers Lane and Vancouver Street, and about 20 derelict boats nearby that he says are dumping sewage and fuel
Hundreds of overweight trucks carrying port cargo through downtown instead of by rail
Food trucks taking up to four downtown parking stalls and running generators, when a food-truck court with power already exists
Council criticising LNG “but does nothing themselves except switch to LED lights”
Campaign signs and political donations for his own campaign — says he accepts none

growth.position: In the middle on pace; strongly against taller buildings downtown; “high density, low sprawl” family housing
growth.summary: Wants the town to grow beyond one- and two-bedroom downtown condos, with family housing on the Cheema lands, and says parking and road access (a second route into downtown) must keep up.
growth.quote: This will enable our town to grow beyond one- and two bedroom downtown condos.

housing_affordability.position: Whistler-style housing authority; against requiring a below-market share in big projects; keep District land for housing
housing_affordability.summary: Would copy Whistler’s 30-year-old housing authority: homes with covenants on rents and caps on resale prices so locals can buy in and seniors can downsize without leaving town. Would convert vacant required office space in residential buildings to affordable and seniors’ housing, and lobby the Province and Ottawa for affordable and seniors’ housing.
housing_affordability.quote: I will constantly and always advocate to the provincial and federal governments for affordable and senior housing.

homelessness.position: Keep Under One Roof where it is, but clear the encampments and move the injection site; against more shelters near homes
homelessness.summary: Says the safe injection site must be moved away from the library, a daycare, a park and homes, and asks why a trailer-and-tent encampment on a private vacant lot is allowed and whether the owner is being fined.
homelessness.quote: The safe injection site needs to be removed from its location beside our public library, Montessori daycare, park, and local residents.

policing.position: More foot patrols and bylaw officers downtown; bylaws against open drug use — “a strong arm”
policing.summary: Describes being attacked downtown with a wooden spear, a pipe, needles and rocks.

taxes_spending.position: Take the Woodfibre tax deal and put it toward Brennan Park; borrow to renew Brennan Park; in the middle on holding taxes down
taxes_spending.summary: Argues that small maintenance spending now (weeds, curbs, drains) saves large repair bills later, that heavy trucks are wrecking downtown roads at taxpayers’ cost, and that Woodfibre LNG and senior governments should help fund local projects. No property-tax target stated.
taxes_spending.quote: For a minor maintenance cost now, we will save the future tax base from the high costs of replacing our roads and streetscapes.

environment_lng.position: Take the Woodfibre tax deal, but press the plant on local impacts; climate a top priority — solar on public buildings
environment_lng.summary: A renewable-energy advocate who nonetheless says Squamish should work with the LNG company to help fund community projects, and criticises council for complaining about LNG while doing little itself. Wants renewable energy on municipal buildings, schools and new construction.
environment_lng.quote: Contrary to my beliefs as a renewable energy advocate, we need to work with the LNG company, which can help financially support various projects in our community.

transportation.position: Against local tax dollars for regional transit (wants a local gas tax instead); for bike lanes and sidewalks
transportation.summary: Pave and open Bailey Street as a second route into downtown; buy the Loggers Lane rail line to extend the bike lane and add permit parking; run a winter bus to Darrell Bay; work with neighbouring towns on Sea to Sky transit; keep heavy port cargo on rail rather than downtown roads.
transportation.quote: One bad accident on Cleveland Avenue and traffic across the whole town grinds to a halt.

economy.position: Referendums on big projects; in the middle on cutting red tape
economy.summary: No specific plan for jobs or business. Wants port cargo moved by rail instead of trucks through downtown, and food trucks moved to the food-truck court rather than taking street parking.

parking.position: New buildings must supply parking; against paid parking — visitors only, locals free, once Loggers Lane parking exists
parking.summary: His press release calls parking 'an ongoing problem in all neighbourhoods'. He would acquire the rail line on Loggers Lane to extend the bike lane and 'create angled parking that is paid for by visitors but available to our residents and employees with a permit', pave overflow parking for Bailey Street residents, and says 'Builders need to supply sufficient parking instead of opting for cash-in-lieu', suggesting vacant lots be cleaned up as temporary parking. He objects to food trucks 'taking up to four parking stalls each' downtown.
parking.quote: Builders need to supply sufficient parking instead of opting for cash-in-lieu, and they must maintain their vacant land. They could clean up their lots to create temporary parking solutions.

compass.rationale: No public statements, platform, media profile or voting record were found, so there is no evidence on which to place him. Values are set to zero as a placeholder, not as a finding that he is centrist.

name: Shaun Veltkamp
occupation_background: Squamish business owner for 20+ years (listed as 'of The Hive MediaWorks' on the Tourism Squamish board) who says he has run over 100 international projects. Moved to the Sea to Sky Corridor in 1990; describes himself as a two-term elected director on the Tourism Squamish board and a volunteer youth sports coach.
tagline: “Prepared to do the hard work — we have to make good decisions.”
top_priorities: Housing Affordability
Environment & Green Spaces
Trades & Local Jobs
Transit & Infrastructure
Families & Community Services
Transparent Local Government

supports.text: More attainable housing options, 'sensible density near transit' and protections for renters
Hiring the best possible Chief Administrative Officer and reviewing/refocusing the Official Community Plan
Aggressively pursuing provincial and federal funding for a new community centre, a hospital and an alternate access route to downtown
Revitalizing the District's Economic Development Department
Cutting unnecessary red tape for local contractors, tradespeople and small businesses
Better bus service, safer roads, and reliable water and sewer infrastructure
Investing in childcare, recreation and community programs
Protecting the natural environment and public access to the outdoors as development proceeds
Council listening to qualified experts, using reliable data and weighing costs and benefits before major decisions

opposes.text: Housing supply that is 'just luxury condos'
Taking donations for his own campaign: says it is 100% self-financed and will accept no donations of any kind

growth.position: In the middle on pace; hold building heights and the growth boundary for now
growth.summary: Says rapid growth has brought 'real pressure on housing, infrastructure, and the character of the community'; wants the OCP reviewed and refocused and infrastructure put first, while supporting 'sensible density near transit'.
growth.quote: That growth has brought opportunity but also real pressure on housing, infrastructure, and the character of the community.

housing_affordability.position: More attainable housing, density near transit, renter protections
housing_affordability.summary: Says workers and families are being priced out and calls for more attainable housing options, sensible density near transit and protections for renters.
housing_affordability.quote: We need more attainable housing options, sensible density near transit, and protections for renters — not just luxury condos.

homelessness.position: More shelter space, and move Under One Roof out of downtown
homelessness.summary: Shaun had said little in public about this before answering our questionnaire. Shaun’s own answers are below.

policing.summary: Shaun had said little in public about this before answering our questionnaire. Shaun’s own answers are below.

taxes_spending.position: Build a new community centre, paid for mainly by senior government and industry, not local tax increases
taxes_spending.summary: Emphasizes taxpayer dollars spent responsibly, clear priorities, and cost-benefit evaluation before major decisions; wants provincial and federal funding pursued for a new community centre, hospital and alternate downtown access.
taxes_spending.quote: My goal is to ensure taxpayer dollars are spent responsibly, priorities are clear, and important projects move forward efficiently and with long-term value for our community.

transportation.summary: Lists better bus service and safer roads as basics, and wants senior-government funding for an alternate access route to downtown.

economy.summary: Wants to support local contractors, tradespeople and small businesses, cut unnecessary red tape, revitalize the Economic Development Department, and keep Squamish 'welcoming for tourists'. Sits on the Tourism Squamish board.
economy.quote: Cut unnecessary red tape so Squamish workers can build their futures right here in the Sea to Sky corridor.
